content.p: Two middle-school friends, 13-year-old Abby Williams and 14-year-old Libby German, went for a walk along a hiking trail outside Delphi, Indiana, on 13 February 2017, a day off from school. Their bodies were found the next day. For more than five years the case turned on a blurred figure in a phone video, whom investigators called "Bridge Guy".

In October 2022 police arrested Richard Allen, a local pharmacy technician. A jury convicted him on 11 November 2024, and on 20 December Special Judge Frances Gull sentenced him to 130 years, the most the law allowed. Allen says he is innocent. His appeal was argued in front of the Indiana Court of Appeals on 21 September 2026, and the panel took the case under advisement.
content.h2: The walk on the Monon High Bridge
content.p: A&E's account says that Libby's older sister dropped the girls at a trailhead on the Delphi Historic Trails, a network of paths linking the town to Deer Creek and the Wabash River. NBC News put the town's population at around 2,900. Libby posted a photograph on social media of Abby crossing the Monon High Bridge. When the girls did not meet Libby's father at the arranged time, their families searched and then called police. The bodies were found the following day in woods about half a mile from the bridge, according to authorities quoted by CNN. Both had died from cuts to the throat, and an unspent .40-caliber cartridge was found between them.

According to the police affidavit that was unsealed in November 2022, the girls were dropped off just before 1:50 p.m. and the video shows them meeting a man at the bridge at 2:13 p.m. The man, in a dark jacket and jeans, walks behind them and says "Guys, down the hill". Other reports of the recording quote the words as "Girls, down the hill". A later witness told investigators she saw a man heading away from the bridge shortly before 4 p.m., "muddy and bloody".

In February 2017 police released two grainy stills from the video and an audio recording of the muffled voice. They issued a sketch in July 2017 and a different one in April 2019. A reward fund that volunteers contributed to passed $224,000 by the end of March 2017, and more than 11,000 tips arrived. Officials called Libby a hero for recording what she did. In December 2021, state police asked for information about a fictitious online profile, "anthony_shots", used with young girls in 2016 and 2017.

Police followed many leads, and a handful of people were charged with other offences. A man named Kegan Kline admitted communicating online with Libby and dozens of other teenage girls and pleaded guilty to child-exploitation offences, A&E reported, but, in A&E's words, no real evidence linked him to the deaths.

The break came by accident. In September 2022 a volunteer working through tip files, Kathy Shank, noticed a tip marked "clear" that should not have been. It recorded that Allen, a Delphi resident, told a state conservation officer within days of the killings that he had been on the trail that afternoon. Carroll County Sheriff Tony Liggett said Allen had "got lost in the cracks". Investigators executed a search warrant at his home on 13 October 2022 and took firearms, knives, jackets and boots. Lab tests, according to the affidavit, showed the cartridge from the scene had been cycled through his Sig Sauer .40-caliber pistol. He was arrested on 26 October 2022 and was charged with two counts of murder, and the prosecutors added two more murder counts later. He pleaded not guilty.
content.h2: The fight over the defence team
content.p: The case nearly lost its first set of defenders before trial. In October 2023 Judge Gull removed Allen's court-appointed lawyers, Andrew Baldwin and Brad Rozzi, after crime scene photographs were leaked from Baldwin's office. A former employee of the firm admitted taking pictures of the photos without Baldwin's knowledge and was criminally charged. Gull said the leak was one of several examples of gross negligence by the lawyers and accused them of making false statements.

The Indiana Supreme Court decided on 18 January 2024 to reinstate Baldwin and Rozzi. It said the trial court had not found their removal a necessary last resort after weighing the prejudice to Allen. The justices kept Gull on the case, unanimously, finding Allen had not shown she was biased.

Opening statements were on 18 October 2024. McLeland told the jury the state's case rested on three things: the killings, the video of the man known as "Bridge Guy", and the unspent cartridge. He later said Allen was Bridge Guy and had killed the girls. The state also relied on witnesses who had seen a man on the trail. One of them, a teenager, said she said hello to a man who looked overdressed for the weather, in a hat, mask and dark clothing.

The confessions were central. Prosecutors said Allen admitted the killings more than 60 times, to his wife, his mother, a prison psychologist, the warden, prison staff and inmates. The jury heard a jail call in which he told his wife, "I did it, I killed Abby. I killed Abby and Libby." NBC News noted that his wife seemed not to believe him, telling him the medication might be affecting his thinking. Monica Wala, the former lead psychologist at Westville Correctional Facility, testified that Allen first told her he was innocent and began confessing in April 2023, around the time he went back on suicide watch.

The defence argued there was no DNA or other physical evidence connecting Allen to the girls, no one had identified him as the man in the video, and the confessions were false, born of months in solitary confinement and a deteriorating mind. Rozzi told the jury it should acquit. The defence stressed that a hair found with one of the girls belonged to neither of them and did not match Allen's DNA. Judge Gull barred the defence from showing the jury the two police sketches. According to prosecutors, Allen volunteered to police that he had been on the trail during the period when the girls disappeared. The defence suggested he had already left by the time the girls arrived and said he often walked there.
After about 19 hours of deliberation, the sequestered jury of 12 found Allen guilty on all four counts: two of murder and two of murder committed in the course of a kidnapping.

Allen, then 52, was sentenced on 20 December 2024. He faced between 45 and 130 years. Gull imposed 65 years on each of two counts, to be served one after the other. She said she had spent 27 years as a judge and that "you rank right up there with the most heinous crimes in the state of Indiana." She added, "These families will deal with your carnage forever." Six relatives of the girls gave victim-impact statements. Libby's grandfather, Mike Patty, said that "justice has been served for the girls." Libby's uncle, Cody Patty, said "this still ain't justice" and called it "a little closure". The prosecutor McLeland thanked Libby for recording the man on the bridge, and Abby for hiding the phone from the killer so police could find it, a claim he made in his press conference. Allen's lawyers said he would appeal.

By May 2026 Allen's appeal had been filed, and the Court of Appeals had granted his lawyers' request for oral argument. The hearing took place on 21 September 2026 at the Supreme Court courtroom in the Indiana Statehouse, before Judges Vaidik, Altice and Brown. His attorney Mark Leeman and Deputy Attorney General Ellen Meilaender each had 30 minutes.

The defence raised three issues: that the search of his home was unconstitutional because, it says, police left out or changed witness descriptions to make Allen resemble the man in the video; that his confessions were coerced by "unprecedented confinement", including time in a cell known as "the Hole"; and that the trial court denied him a complete defence by excluding evidence pointing elsewhere. Leeman argued the crime scene suggested effort and planning that sat "uneasy" with the state's theory of one man acting on impulse. He pointed to other possible suspects, including Brad Holder, and the lawyers also argued over the theory that the girls were killed in a ritual tied to Odinism, which, 21Alive reported, police investigated in the early stages. These are the defence's theories; the trial court excluded them and the state disputes them.

Meilaender said Allen was kept on suicide watch in restrictive housing for his own safety, with recreation, medical checks, a tablet and visits from his wife, and that he had confessed to his wife, his mother and a doctor when "very lucid, very coherent". She called his statements to police identifying himself as the man the girls saw "the most powerful evidence" the state had, and said the timeline, eyewitnesses and his own statements proved he was Bridge Guy. Judges pressed the state on whether holding a presumed-innocent detainee in such conditions was coercive. The panel took the case under advisement, and a written decision could take months.
